---
title: "Hierarchical outcomes after stem cell transplant: a worked example"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(hpsreg)
```

## Idea

Patients after allogeneic transplant experience several outcomes of unequal importance.
Instead of collapsing them into one composite event, a *hierarchy* ranks the outcomes:
for any two patients the first level that separates them decides who did better.
`hpsreg` has three stages: **design** the hierarchy, **score** all pairs, **estimate**.

## 1. Data

```{r data}
dat <- simulate_hps(N = 613, seed = 20241003)
dim(dat)
head(dat[, c("donor_type", "age", "dri", "death_day", "relapse_day", "gvhd_grade")])
```

`NA` in a `*_day` column means the event did not occur by day 180.

## 2. Design the hierarchy from the data-frame variables

Survival, then relapse, then GVHD (grade, then resolution, then onset), then infection.
Each level names a column of `dat` and states which direction is favourable.

* `lvl_tte()` reads "time of the event, `NA` if it did not occur", so a patient with no
  death is better than any patient who died, and a later death is better than an earlier one.
* `lvl_group()` bundles several comparisons into one reported level.
* `when = "..."` is an eligibility guard: resolution and onset are compared only between
  patients who had GVHD (pairs where either patient is ineligible pass to the next level).

```{r hier-scratch}
h <- hierarchy(
  lvl_tte("death_day",   better = "later", name = "survival"),
  lvl_tte("relapse_day", better = "later", name = "relapse"),
  lvl_group("GVHD",
    lvl_ordinal("gvhd_grade", better = "lower", name = "grade"),
    lvl_binary("gvhd_resolved", favorable = 1, when = "gvhd_grade > 0",
               name = "resolution"),
    lvl_continuous("gvhd_onset_day", better = "higher", when = "gvhd_grade > 0",
                   name = "onset")),
  lvl_group("infection",
    lvl_ordinal("infection_grade", better = "lower", name = "grade"),
    lvl_binary("infection_resolved", favorable = 1, when = "infection_grade > 0",
               name = "resolution"))
)
h
```

The package ships this hierarchy as `hps_hierarchy()`; the two are identical:

```{r hier-shortcut}
identical(score_pairs(h, dat)$W, score_pairs(hps_hierarchy(), dat)$W)
```

## 3. Score pairs

```{r score}
pw <- score_pairs(h, dat)
pw
resolution(pw)
resolution(pw, by = "leaf")
```

## 4. Covariate-adjusted analysis

`btd()` can use the pairs computed above (`pairs = pw`), so several covariate models share
one scoring pass, or it can score them itself (`hierarchy = h`).

```{r fit}
fit <- btd(~ donor_type + age + dri + hct_ci + sex_mismatch + year +
             conditioning + cell_source, data = dat, pairs = pw)
summary(fit)
```

```{r fit-inline}
fit_inline <- btd(~ donor_type + age, data = dat, hierarchy = h)   # scores internally
fit_reuse  <- btd(~ donor_type + age, data = dat, pairs = pw)      # reuses pw
all.equal(coef(fit_inline), coef(fit_reuse))
```

Positive coefficients mean a better position in the hierarchy. Standard errors are
sandwich estimates that account for each patient appearing in many pairs.

## 5. Comparison with a composite Cox analysis

The conventional analysis uses the composite m-GRFS event. A Cox log hazard ratio has the
opposite orientation (higher hazard = worse), so we compare with the sign reversed.

```{r cox}
covars <- c("donor_type", "age", "dri", "hct_ci", "sex_mismatch", "year",
            "conditioning", "cell_source")
cx <- hps_cox_grfs(dat, covars)
cmp <- data.frame(term = names(coef(fit)),
                  btd = unname(coef(fit)), btd_se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))),
                  neg_cox = -unname(cx$coef), cox_se = unname(cx$se))
cmp[-1] <- round(cmp[-1], 3)
cmp
```

## 6. Unadjusted win statistics and diagnostics

```{r win}
win_stats(pw, dat$year)
```

Does one latent scale describe all levels? Among pairs decided at each level, the
observed win rate should match the model's prediction.

```{r calib}
btd_calibration(fit)
btd_calibration(fit, by = "bin", n_bins = 5)
```

## 7. Other endpoint types

The hierarchy module does not know about transplant. A trial with a censored
time-to-event endpoint, an ordinal score, a continuous marker with a clinically
meaningful margin, and a binary event:

```{r other}
set.seed(1)
n <- 150
trial <- data.frame(
  arm    = rep(c("control", "treatment"), each = n / 2),
  age    = round(rnorm(n, 60, 8)),
  time   = rexp(n, 0.02), cens = runif(n, 20, 120)
)
trial$status <- as.integer(trial$time <= trial$cens)
trial$time   <- pmin(trial$time, trial$cens)
trial$score  <- sample(0:3, n, TRUE, prob = c(.4, .3, .2, .1))
trial$marker <- rnorm(n, 10 - (trial$arm == "treatment"), 2)
trial$ae     <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)

h2 <- hierarchy(
  lvl_tte("time", status = "status", better = "later", name = "OS"),
  lvl_ordinal("score", better = "lower", name = "severity"),
  lvl_continuous("marker", better = "lower", threshold = 1, name = "marker"),
  lvl_binary("ae", favorable = 0, name = "no adverse event")
)
pw2 <- score_pairs(h2, trial)
pw2
resolution(pw2)
win_stats(pw2, trial$arm, treatment = "treatment")
```

Pairs whose ordering is unknown because of censoring are passed to the next level and flagged
(`pw2$uninf`). This Gehan-type rule is biased toward the null under heavy censoring.

```{r other-fit}
summary(btd(~ I(arm == "treatment") + age, trial, pairs = pw2))
```

## 8. Custom levels

```{r custom}
by_sign <- function(data, i, j) sign(data$marker[j] - data$marker[i])
h3 <- hierarchy(lvl_binary("ae", favorable = 0), lvl_custom(by_sign, "marker (R function)"))
resolution(score_pairs(h3, trial))
```
